RegexExtract | structured data preservation | The 'All Groups' mode in RegexExtract.execute() may include None values in the join operation when match.groups() exists but the group_index is out of bounds for a specific match. The code checks `len(match.groups()) >= group_index` but then calls `match.group(group_index)` without ensuring the group is not None. In Python regex, groups can be None when they don't participate in the match. Additionally, the 'All Matches' mode only extracts the first element (m[0]) from tuple matches, potentially losing data from other capture groups.

Post-context evidence: Digest confirms Python regex groups can return None when optional groups don't match. The code checks len(match.groups()) >= group_index but doesn't check if the group value is None before appending to results list. str.join() will raise TypeError if results contains None values. This is a concrete crash defect supported by static analysis. runtime unverified (harness)
recommendation: Preserve the relevant captured values from each structured match row, or make the single-slot contract explicit in code.

content: In 'All Matches' mode, the code assumes matches[0] is either a tuple or a string. However, re.findall returns different structures depending on whether the pattern has capturing groups. If the pattern has multiple groups, matches[0] will be a tuple, but the code only extracts m[0], potentially losing data.
recommendation: Clarify the intended behavior for multi-group patterns. Consider either flattening all groups or providing separate output for each group index.
